<p align="center"><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skizzophrenic/SquachWatch-CYD/v1.6.0/docs/squachmesh-emotes.gif" width="640" alt="A visiting Squachy arrives; the message screen opens, the emote picker shows its tabs, a pie is picked and lands on the visitor's face; the visitor sends rock-paper-scissors back and both hands are revealed; then eight Squachys drift about the screen in two rows."></p>

**Twenty-nine new emotes, and a crowd.** Two SquachWatches can now do thirty-five different things to each other from the message screen, and a room full of them puts everybody on screen at once. There is also a hat. Details below, and at the bottom, the story of the bug that took an entire evening and two boards swapped on one USB port more times than either of us wants to count.

## Emotes

The message screen has an EMOTE button in the corner now. Behind it are six tabs — HI, PLAY, PRANK, PARTY, MOOD, WATCH — of up to six emotes each: a wave, a high five, a fist bump, a secret handshake, a salute, a bow, rock-paper-scissors, a coin flip, dice, an arm wrestle, a tug of war, leapfrog, a snowball, a pie, a water balloon, a paper plane, a pillow fight, a hug, a gift, a snack, cheers, confetti, fireworks, a dance, a heart, a laugh, a sulk, a growl, a nap, a tinfoil hat, a camera, "did you see that?", a howl, and a selfie. RANDOM picks one for you.

**Both boards act it out.** Tap one and your Squachy does it to the visitor on your screen while, on theirs, their Squachy has it done to them by you. Whoever sent it goes first, so the two screens tell the same story from their two sides.

**The contests are real, and they agree.** Rock-paper-scissors, the coin, the dice, the arm wrestle and the tug of war all have a winner, and it is the same winner on both boards. The sending board rolls once and the result rides along inside the emote, so nobody is looking at a different game. It really is best of one.

**An emote interrupts.** If the two of them are in the middle of a dance-off or a nap when one arrives, they stop and do the emote. Somebody pressed a button and is watching for it; the set pieces start themselves and can wait.

**Older firmware ignores them.** Messages are unchanged and still work with v1.5.24 and v1.5.25 boards. Emotes are a new kind of frame those builds do not read, so they drop one quietly rather than show something they cannot place. Update both boards.

## The crowd

**Settings → SQUACHMESH → CROWD.** Set it past ONE and everybody in range is on screen at once — up to eight, which is as many as the radio keeps track of. They shrink to fit and drift about their own patch of the screen; nobody stands on the floor, yours included, and yours holds the middle so you can always find him.

**The shape follows the headcount.** Up to four stand in one row. Five is three behind and two in front, six is three and three, seven is four and three, eight is four and four. Each count is drawn as large as its shape allows: three of them are half again the size of eight, and four are a fifth larger.

**Names come off past four.** Up to four they all wear nameplates; more than that and the nameplates are the clutter, so they go, and a tap on any Squachy puts his name up for a few seconds instead.

**It is cheaper than two.** Measured on a board: eight of them at the size they land on cost 17.6 ms a frame to draw, against 29 ms for the ordinary pair at full size. Drawing cost follows the area they cover, not how many there are.

**Set pieces and emotes stand down while a crowd is up.** Both are written for exactly two Squachys on fixed marks, and there are no marks in a crowd. With one visitor — CROWD set to ONE, or a crowd setting with only one other board around — everything works as before.

**Two is not on the menu**, because two is one visitor, and one visitor is the ordinary visit with all its choreography, which is better than a crowd of two would be. The setting goes ONE, then 3 through 8.

## Squachy

**He drops hints.** On the backgrounds that hide something, he now says so — vaguely at first, and less vaguely the longer you stand there without finding it. He will not tell you outright. He wants you to find it.

**A top hat at Legend.** Reach the last growth stage and he wears a top hat, seated properly on every outfit — on the dome of the space suit, between the wolf pelt's ears, up through the unicorn's horn. **Settings → SQUACHY → APPEARANCE → TOP HAT** takes it off, and the row only appears once he has one.

**APPEARANCE is its own page.** Theme, background, brightness, invert, colour order, rotation lock, shades colour and the hat live behind one row under SQUACHY, instead of eight rows at the top of Settings that were the first thing under your thumb. Boring mode keeps the page — it is how you reach brightness.

**The squad badge moved.** How many SquachWatches are in range now sits bottom right above the counters, thumb-sized, and opens the SQUAD screen.

## The bug hunt

The emotes worked in the emulator on the first day. They worked from the sending board on the first day. On the receiving board, nothing. The frame arrived, decrypted, logged itself politely — and then vanished without acting anything out.

Over one long evening this was, in order: definitely the CROWD setting refusing emotes (it was, and that is fixed, but it was not this); definitely the receive path throwing an emote away before checking whether it could use it (it was, and that is fixed, but it was not this either); definitely the phase machine only looking for emotes in the last of six phases (also true, also fixed, also not this); definitely the peer's address not matching; definitely the draw loop not running on every frame; and at one point, definitely the phrase not being set, which it was, twice.

Every one of those was reasoned out by reading the source, and every one was wrong about the symptom. Two boards were swapped on and off a single USB port roughly a dozen times, nine builds were flashed, and the emulator — asked to reproduce the fault four different ways — played every emote perfectly each time, which should have been the clue.

The bug was eight milliseconds long. The main loop reads the clock once at the top of each pass. A received emote is decrypted and queued a few milliseconds later, and stamps itself from the clock again — so its timestamp sat slightly in the future of the loop's idea of now. Subtracting a future time from a past one on an unsigned integer does not give a small negative number; it gives four billion. Four billion milliseconds is older than twelve seconds, so the emote was expired in the same call that queued it. The emulator's clock does not move within a frame, so it never saw it. The sending board queues on one pass and checks on the next, when now has caught up, so it never saw it either. Only a real receiver, on a real clock, ever could.

One comparison made signed, and it worked. The GIF at the top is the shipping firmware playing the very first pie.

## Also in this release

The web emulator has the emotes: bring the virtual SquachWatch nearby, open the message screen, and try the picker. It has one virtual SquachWatch, so the crowd needs real boards.

The crowd was measured on hardware before it was built. The numbers, and the test build that produced them, are in the repo under `crowd_bench`.
